lesson.title: Not Just a Collision: The Orientation Factor
lesson.summary: Even a collision that carries enough energy to react can still fail if the molecules meet at the wrong angle; the orientation factor measures how much molecular geometry limits a reaction's rate.
lesson.body:
You already know from effective collisions that two things have to go right for a reaction to happen: the colliding particles need enough kinetic energy to get over the activation energy barrier, and they need to hit each other in a geometry that actually lines up the atoms that are going to form new bonds. Energy gets most of the attention in introductory treatments, but geometry is just as real a filter. A fast-moving molecule that slams into its partner backward, or off to the side, simply bounces away unchanged, no matter how much energy it was carrying.

Think about a reaction like NO plus Cl2, where a nitrogen atom needs to end up bonded to a chlorine atom. If the NO molecule approaches Cl2 nitrogen-first, the new bond can form. If it approaches oxygen-first, the reactive nitrogen is pointed the wrong way and the collision is wasted, even at high energy. Bigger, more complicated molecules make this worse: a large organic molecule might have only one small reactive patch on its surface, so most of the ways it can tumble into a partner molecule simply do not present that patch.

Chemists capture this idea with the orientation factor, usually written p (sometimes called the steric factor). It is defined as the fraction of sufficiently energetic collisions that also happen to have a workable geometry, and it is calculated by comparing the rate constant collision theory predicts if geometry did not matter at all to the rate constant actually measured in the lab:

p = k(observed) / k(predicted from energy and collision frequency alone)

Suppose collision theory, using only the size of the molecules, their average speed, and the fraction with energy above Ea, predicts a rate constant of about 2.0 times 10 to the 11th power L/(mol times s) if every sufficiently energetic collision reacted. If the rate constant actually measured in the lab is 3.0 times 10 to the 9th power L/(mol times s), then

p = (3.0 x 10^9) / (2.0 x 10^11) = 0.015

Only about 1.5 percent of the collisions that clear the energy hurdle also happen to be oriented correctly. That is a fully worked, self-consistent illustration of how p is calculated, not a claim about any one specific real reaction's measured rate constants.

The value of p always falls between 0 and 1, and its size tells you something physical about the reacting species. For very small, nearly spherical particles, such as two atoms colliding to form a diatomic molecule, almost any orientation works, so p is close to 1. For larger, more structured molecules, p can be far smaller, sometimes down around one in a million or less, because only a narrow slice of all possible approach angles brings the reactive atoms together correctly. Keep p in mind as you move into the next few chapters: it is one of the two ingredients, along with how often molecules collide in the first place, that combine to form what chemists call the frequency factor in the Arrhenius equation.
